extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent attorneys/agents, and claim drafters preparing independent claims (USPTO practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidance for the architecture and wording of an independent patent claim, covering structure (preamble/transition/body), verb choice, antecedent basis, actor attribution, and claim length heuristics. Aimed at producing defensible, examinable independent claims in U.S. prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim architecture: three layers (preamble, transition, body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every well-drafted independent claim has three layers: (1) the preamble, which states what the claim is for; (2) the transition, which sets the scope ("comprising," "consisting of," "consisting essentially of"); and (3) the body, which lists the elements/limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design claims with clear separation of these layers so each performs its drafting function (preamble states purpose/context, transition sets openness, body recites elements/limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble limitingness
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble is generally not limiting unless it (a) breathes life and meaning into the claim, (b) provides antecedent basis for terms in the body, or (c) was relied upon during prosecution to distinguish prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat every preamble as a potential limitation; avoid marketing language in the preamble. If the preamble supplies essential context or antecedent terms, it may be construed as limiting. Be cautious that statements made during prosecution relying on the preamble can create prosecution-history-based limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition choice: openness of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comprising" is open: the claim covers anything containing the listed elements plus more. "Consisting of" is closed: only the listed elements. "Consisting essentially of" is semi-closed: listed elements plus things that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to "comprising" unless there is a tactical reason to limit scope (e.g., to exclude certain materials or steps). Choose transition deliberately to control claim breadth and exclusion of unrecited features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element order in the body
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements should appear in an order that supports the function of the invention - typically the order in which they interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciting elements in the order they operate makes the claim easier to read and easier to argue. Avoid haphazard ordering that frustrates comprehension and prosecution/claim-construction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Each noun in a claim should be introduced with "a" or "an" once, then referred to with "the" or "said" thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide proper antecedent basis (e.g., using "the widget" without first reciting "a widget") invites 35 U.S.C. §112(b)/indefiniteness rejections. Maintain consistent introduction and subsequent reference forms to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active voice verbs in method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Each step in a method claim should use an active verb: "applying," "determining," "transmitting," "decoding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid passive constructions (e.g., "the signal is received") because they make it ambiguous who performs the step and can create divided-infringement issues. Active verbs clarify the actor and reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-actor drafting for method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims should be drafted so a single actor performs every step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because divided-infringement doctrines (e.g., Akamai v. Limelight) make proving infringement by multiple parties difficult, the easiest defense is to write claims so one entity performs all steps. Where multiple parties may be involved, consider drafting system/apparatus claims or including agent language to attribute acts to a single entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Whereby" clause caution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whereby" clauses describe results. They are usually held to be non-limiting (Texas Instruments v. ITC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "whereby" clauses sparingly. Do not rely on them to distinguish prior art—move substantive distinguishing material into affirmative claim limitations rather than a result-oriented "whereby" clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length-of-claim heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that takes more than a single page in 12-point single-spaced text is almost always too narrow. A claim that takes less than 4 lines is almost always too broad to survive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a claim of moderate length—neither extremely short nor excessively long. Use this heuristic as a quick check on likely prosecution survivability: target somewhere between 4 lines and one page in 12-pt single-spaced text.
